# Graphite changes to Textual 0.5.0

Upstream: https://github.com/gonzalezreal/textual at tag 0.5.0 (commit 01b51875a5406eefc95f52a058cb059e7bc94dc4). License: MIT (see LICENSE); third-party notices in LICENSE-3rdparty.csv. Upstream tests, examples and documentation are not vendored. Textual's SwiftUIMath dependency is Graphite's vendored copy (`Vendor/swiftui-math`, with its own `GRAPHITE-PATCHES.md`), not the remote package.

## 1. Math keeps its natural width

`Sources/Textual/Internal/Attachment/MathAttachment.swift`: inline math is measured without a width limit and drawn at its natural width (`fixedSize`). Upstream fits it to the proposed width. When a formula is the whole content of a table cell, the frame it receives is a fraction of a point narrower than the formula, so formulas such as `$k_n$` or `$x_n$` (letters with subscript kerning) line-broke inside the formula and rendered as garbled glyphs. Display math had the same problem (`E = mc^2` drew its exponent on a second line), so it is also measured and drawn at its natural width, and fitted to the proposed width only when it is wider than that by more than one point (`MathAttachment.naturalWidthTolerance`), the same tolerance the view draws with, so the size reserved is the size drawn.

## 2. List item styles can see the item's content

`Sources/Textual/StructuredText/Style/ListItemStyle.swift`, `Internal/StructuredText/UnorderedList.swift`, `Internal/StructuredText/OrderedList.swift`: `ListItemStyleConfiguration` gains a public `content` (the item's `AttributedSubstring`). Graphite's list item style uses it to draw a task's checkbox in place of the bullet, as Obsidian does.

## 3. Inline math for other text views

`Sources/Textual/InlineMathRendering.swift` (new): public `InlineMathRendering.metrics(for:fontSize:)` and `image(for:fontSize:color:scale:)`, which measure and draw a formula with the same font and typesetting as inline math in `StructuredText`. Graphite's Live Preview editor uses them to draw `$…$` formulas among its own text. They wrap SwiftUIMath API that is only available to Textual (`@_spi(Textual)`).

## 4. Obsidian's inline math delimiters

`Sources/Textual/Internal/MarkdownParser/PatternTokenizer.swift`: `$…$` is inline math only when no space follows the opening `$` or precedes the closing one, and no digit follows the closing one, as in Obsidian. Upstream treats any pair of dollar signs as math, so "It costs $5 and $10" rendered "5 and " as a formula.

## 5. Formulas that cannot be typeset stay as text

`Sources/Textual/MarkdownParser/SyntaxExtension.swift`, `Internal/Attachment/MathAttachment.swift`: when SwiftUIMath cannot parse a formula (for example an unknown command or environment), the math extension leaves its `$…$` source as text. Upstream made an attachment that measured zero and showed only the object replacement glyph.

## 6. No isolated-conformance warnings from attachments

`Sources/Textual/Internal/Attachment/WithAttachments.swift`: the main-actor model that resolves attachments is a top-level type (`AttachmentResolutionModel`) instead of being nested in the generic `WithAttachments<Content>` view. Nested, it carried the view's `Content: View` conformance, and Swift 6.2 warned five times that the conformance "may be isolated and cannot be passed to main actor-isolated context". Behavior is unchanged.

## 7. Tables fit the width they are offered

`Sources/Textual/Internal/StructuredText/TableColumnsLayout.swift` and `TableCellWidthProbe.swift` (new), `Internal/StructuredText/Table.swift`, `Internal/StructuredText/TableCell.swift`, `Internal/TextFragment/TextFragment.swift`, `Internal/TextFragment/TextBuilder.swift`: a table is laid out by `TableColumnsLayout` in place of SwiftUI's `Grid`. Upstream's table never adapted to its width in a usable way. `Grid` gives a column the width its widest cell asks for, and a `Text` accepts any width down to one letter per line, so a table offered less width than its content either kept its full width or broke words apart. An image in a cell was sized to the whole text container, not to its column, so three images side by side made a table three containers wide.

The layout sizes columns as a web browser sizes a table:

- A column is at most as wide as its widest cell on one line, and at least as wide as the widest word, formula, or smallest image in it.
- A table offered a width between those limits gives each column the same share of the width it can give up. Widths are whole points.
- A table offered less than its narrowest width keeps that width, so the style's scroll container scrolls.

The limits are measured on hidden copies of a cell (`TableCellWidthProbe`), because the visible cell cannot report them: the narrowest on a copy with each word on its own line and each attachment at its smallest, the widest on a copy on one line with each attachment at its full size. A cell of one word or formula needs no copy, and only a cell whose attachments shrink has the second one. The copies are plain `Text`, hidden from hit testing, accessibility and the text layout preference, so they take no part in selection or links.

A cell's content now fills its column (the column's alignment is applied inside the cell, where `Grid` aligned a cell of its content's width). A cell whose attachments fit the width they are offered passes its content width, in whole points, to its `TextFragment` through the `attachmentContainerWidth` environment value, and the fragment sizes attachments for that width in place of the text container's. `TextBuilder` accepts the proposal when it is created, so a fragment built again when an image loads starts at the column's size. That content width is the width the column offers (`StructuredText.ColumnWidthFrame`, in `TableCell.swift`), never the content's own: a flexible frame takes the width of content wider than offered, so a picture a point wider than the space its column left made the width it was fitted to its own, the picture was fitted again a point narrower, and the two took turns at every layout pass, which kept the main thread busy for good when a note's reading view started at such a table (HUNT-360, 2026-11-16). Tests: `AppProjectTextualPatchTests.testAColumnOffersItsPicturesItsOwnWidthEvenWhenAPictureIsWider` and `TableReadingSwitchHostedTests` (iPad simulator).

A table style decides the width to offer. Upstream's `Overflow` scroll container offers none along its scrolling direction, so a style that wants fitting tables offers the container's width itself, as Graphite's `ObsidianTableStyle` does.

## 8. Empty table cells keep their place

`Sources/Textual/Internal/StructuredText/Table.swift`: `Table.cellContents(in:tableIntent:columnCount:)` gives every row every column. A cell with nothing in it has no text, so the attributed string has no run for it, and a row of such cells has none either. Upstream laid out the cells that have runs one after another, so the header `| | Cutoff | Linear |` put "Cutoff" over the first column, and an empty header row (a common way to write a table without headings) made the first row of data the header. A cell now goes to the row and column its presentation intent names, and a place without a run gets an empty cell. `TableLayout` still receives bounds for every row and column, so the dividers a style draws stay in place.

## 9. Preserve explicit formula colors

`Sources/Textual/Internal/Attachment/MathAttachment.swift` and `Sources/Textual/InlineMathRendering.swift`: use SwiftUIMath's multicolor rendering for explicit LaTeX colors rather than discarding them in monochrome mode. Uncolored attachments keep the inherited foreground style; inline images use their supplied text color as the base. Graphite's `LaTeXCompatibility` separately converts scoped MathJax color declarations before these renderers receive them. A regression test parses and renders the reported purple rank equation and checks colored pixels in both halves.

## 10. Controls inside selectable text receive touches

`Sources/Textual/TextInteractionExclusion.swift` (new): public `textual.excludedFromTextInteraction()` reports a view's frame to the text selection overlay, which leaves it out of hit testing, as the overlay already does for the scrollable regions of `Overflow` (`OverflowFrameKey`). With text selection on, the overlay covers the whole text and takes every touch and click, so a control a style draws inside `StructuredText` was never reached. Graphite's list item style draws a task's checkbox as a button in place of the bullet and uses it.

## 11. Display math for views that lay out a formula themselves

`Sources/Textual/DisplayMathRendering.swift` (new), `Internal/Attachment/MathAttachment.swift`: public `DisplayMathRendering.metrics(for:fontSize:fittingWidth:)` measures a formula as block math is typeset, on one line or broken to a width, and `DisplayMathView` draws it at that size. Graphite lays out a formula with its equation numbers with them. The view draws the formula as a canvas symbol, as an attachment is drawn: a view's frame is rounded to whole pixels, and in a frame a fraction of a point narrower than the formula the typesetter broke `E = mc^2` into two lines, of which only the exponent showed. `NaturalWidthWhenItFits` is no longer private to `MathAttachment.swift`, so the view shares it.

## 12. Temporary reading highlights with exact source locations

`Sources/Textual/ReadingHighlight.swift` (new), `Internal/TextFragment/TextBuilder.swift`, `Internal/TextFragment/TextFragment.swift`: a host can attach a validated `ReadingSourceRangeAttribute` to each word or mathematical attachment. `TextBuilder` carries it into SwiftUI's public `Text.Layout` runs. The reading-highlight modifier draws noninteractive backgrounds from the matching run bounds and optionally reports geometry in the host's named coordinate space. It does not replace selection, change document text, search for repeated words, or reparse attributed text for every spoken-word callback. `AnyAttachment.isMathematics` lets the host distinguish formulas from images while validating its complete source-to-rendered token sequence. Graphite tests actual native layout geometry, repeated-word positions, visible highlight pixels, clearing on Stop, and rendered table/math/callout use. Formula attachments report whole-expression bounds, not individual mathematical terms.

## 13. Rounded backgrounds for runs

`Sources/Textual/RoundedRunBackground.swift` (new), `Internal/TextFragment/TextBuilder.swift`, `Internal/TextFragment/TextFragment.swift`: a host can attach a public `RoundedRunBackgroundAttribute` (a color, a corner radius, a padding and an optional border) to runs of its attributed string. `TextBuilder` carries it into `Text.Layout` runs as it carries the reading-highlight ranges, and the fragment draws one rounded shape per line behind the marked runs, joining neighbouring runs with the same background. The radius is limited to half the shape's height and width, so a large radius gives round ends. SwiftUI's own run background is a plain rectangle; Graphite uses this for an Obsidian theme's tag pills and rounded highlights.

## 14. A host tokenizer for code blocks

`Sources/Textual/CodeSegmenter.swift` (new), `Internal/Highlighter/HighlightedTextFragment.swift`: public `StructuredText.CodeSegment` and `textual.codeSegmenter(_:)`, a closure that splits a code block's text into segments with token types, or returns nil for a language it does not know. When it answers, the block is highlighted with those segments synchronously, kept while the block's text, language, highlighter theme and text environment stay the same; otherwise Textual's own Prism tokenizer runs, asynchronously, as upstream. Graphite's tokenizer is pure Swift and covers languages Prism's bundle lacks (C++, VHDL, Verilog, assembly, MATLAB, LaTeX, …), and colors code the same way as Graphite's editor. Upstream tokenized every block asynchronously in JavaScriptCore, so a block first showed uncolored.

## 15. Math patterns compiled once per thread

`Sources/Textual/Internal/MarkdownParser/PatternTokenizer.swift`: `Pattern.mathBlock` and `Pattern.mathInline` return patterns made once per thread (`CompiledMathPatterns`), with the same regular expressions. Upstream made a new value for every access, and a Swift regular expression literal is parsed and compiled again for each new value; the math syntax extension asks for both for every text it parses, which was about a third of the time spent parsing a rendered block's Markdown (Time Profiler, Live Preview scrolling, 2026-10-17). A `Regex` is not `Sendable` and Markdown is also parsed off the main thread, so each thread keeps its own copy in its thread dictionary.


## 16. Tables scroll only when wider than the column

`Sources/Textual/StructuredText/Style/Overflow.swift`: `Overflow(scrollsOnlyWhenWider:content:)` shows its content without a scroll view while the content fits the width it is offered, and moves it into the horizontal scroll view only when it is wider (by more than half a point); content in the scroll view leaves it once the scroll view is wider than the width the content was found wider than, as when the window grows (comparing the content's own widths in the scroll view switched a table in and out without end, since it passes through other widths there as it is laid out again). The space is measured with a layout that takes exactly the width offered: a flexible frame grew to wider content, which then never measured wider and was centered over the column's edges. Graphite's `ObsidianTableStyle` uses it: every table was in a scroll view, which cost layout and scrolling work for tables that never scroll, and took swipes meant for the note. Code block styles keep the plain initializer, since code wraps instead of growing wider and would never be measured wider. The horizontal scroll view also no longer moves vertically (`scrollBounceBehavior(.basedOnSize, axes: .vertical)`): its content's height, rounded to pixels, could exceed its frame by a fraction, and a swipe moved the table up and down.

Content measured wider moves into the scroll view only if its latest measurement is still wider 300 ms later (`widerCheck`); a measurement that fits again in the meantime cancels the move. After a command from a Live Preview table's menu, its cells drawn again measured wider for one pass, and since only a wider column takes content out of the scroll view again, the table stayed in it for good: the scroll view clipped the table's "+" strips and grips, which sit outside its edges, on the Mac and the iPad alike (2026-11-27).

## 17. Table overlays that take touches

`Sources/Textual/View+Textual.swift`, `InteractiveTableOverlay.swift` (new): `textual.interactiveTableOverlay(content:)` is `tableOverlay(content:)` without `allowsHitTesting(false)`. Graphite's Live Preview places a cell editor and its tap target over a table's cells with it, as Obsidian edits a table's cells in place. Because the overlay keeps the table's taps from the text selection overlay, which follows links, it is also given the cells' links: `content` receives a `StructuredText.TableLinks` next to the `TableLayout`, whose `url(at:)` finds the link under a point in the same coordinates, looked up from the cells' `Text.Layout`s only when asked. The two are read from their own preferences and met in one (`InteractiveTableOverlayKey`), since an overlay reads one preference. A tap on a wikilink in a Live Preview table opened the cell's editor instead of the note. Test: `AppProjectTextualPatchTests.testInteractiveTableOverlayFindsTheLinkUnderAPointOfACell`.

## 18. Attachments at hand are drawn at once

`Sources/Textual/Attachment/AttachmentLoader.swift`, `Internal/Attachment/WithAttachments.swift`: `AttachmentLoader` gains `readyAttachment(for:text:environment:)`, the attachment for a URL when the loader has it without loading (nil by default, as upstream). `WithAttachments` draws a text with those attachments until its asynchronous resolution finishes. Graphite's vault image loader answers from the reading view's image cache, so an image the cache holds shows in the first drawing of its text: a note exported to PDF draws each block a few times in quick succession, which do not wait for the asynchronous load, and a text scrolled back into view no longer shows without its images for a moment.

## 19. No `Canvas` in text: backgrounds, attachments and display math are views

`Sources/Textual/RoundedRunBackground.swift`, `Internal/Attachment/AttachmentView.swift`, `DisplayMathRendering.swift`: a run's rounded background is a `RoundedRectangle` per line, an attachment (an inline formula, an emoji) is its own view framed to its run's typographic bounds, and `DisplayMathView` shows SwiftUIMath's `Math` directly instead of drawing it as a canvas symbol. SwiftUI draws a `Canvas` through RenderBox, which starts a Metal device: a note's rendered blocks then held about 200 MB of graphics memory while the note scrolled on the Mac (twelve canvases in a window peak at 245 MB, the same rows drawn as shapes at 18 MB; measured 2026-10-21). The canvas symbol kept a display formula on one line in a frame a fraction of a point narrower than it; SwiftUIMath's typesetter keeps it on one line within a point of its natural width itself (`DisplayProvider.lineBreakTolerance`). Rendered beside the canvas versions, a formula, a table with inline math and code, and a callout match within anti-aliasing at glyph edges.

## 20. The selection model takes every layout of the text

`Sources/Textual/Internal/TextInteraction/Shared/TextSelectionInteraction.swift`, `TextSelectionModel.swift`, `TextSelectionCoordinator.swift`, `UIKit/UIKitTextLayoutModelUpdater.swift` and `AppKit/AppKitTextLayoutModelUpdater.swift` (new): the text's layouts reach the `TextSelectionModel` through a hidden platform view's `updateUIView` / `updateNSView`, which SwiftUI calls at every update with the latest values. Upstream passed them with `onChange`, and SwiftUI runs an `onChange` action at most once per frame ("onChange(of: AnyTextLayoutCollection) action tried to update multiple times per frame"). A text's layouts change several times in the frame it first appears in: each fragment is first an empty `Text` until its `TextBuilder` exists. The model kept the first, empty, layouts (no lines, so no fragment), and found no link and no text under a tap until some later change laid the text out again, such as opening and closing Settings. In Graphite's reading view on the iPad, a tap on a link right after switching from Live Preview, or after opening a note in the reading view, followed nothing. `.task(id:)` has the same limit (it is built on `onChange`), so it is not an alternative. The same change is proposed upstream in [gonzalezreal/textual#71](https://github.com/gonzalezreal/textual/pull/71).

A view update must not change observed state, so carrying a selection over to new layouts updates the stored range without notifying observers: it is the same text, the views that draw the selection read it again with their new layouts, and the platform view is told through `selectionWillChange` and `selectionDidChange`. The coordinator's list of registered models is not observed, since a model registers during an update and no view reads the list. Test: the hosted iPad `ReadingLinkFollowingTests.testTapOnALinkRightAfterSwitchingFromLivePreviewFollowsIt` (a tap delivered through UIKit's event path on a link of the reading view, right after the switch from Live Preview), which fails without the patch, and `PagePreviewCardHostedTests.testATapOnALinkInsideTheCardOpensItsNote` (a tap on a link inside Page Preview's card, whose text is the reading view's), which fails without it too (checked 2026-11-12). A package test cannot show the defect: on the Mac, a selectable text hosted in a window, alone or as the reading view's text, with one paragraph or forty, has its layouts in one update, so `onChange` passed them too.

## 21. Inline math breaks after its operators

`Sources/Textual/Internal/Attachment/InlineMathLineBreaks.swift` (new), `Internal/Attachment/MathAttachment.swift`, `MarkdownParser/SyntaxExtension.swift`, `ReadingHighlight.swift`, `Internal/StructuredText/TableCellWidthProbe.swift`: inline math is drawn in pieces where a line may break, as TeX and MathJax break it: after a binary operator or a relation at the formula's outer level, never inside a group, a `\left…\right` pair, an environment, a script or a root's index, never after a sign (`-x`) or between two relations (`:=`). Each piece ends with the space TeX puts after its operator (`\>` after a binary operator, `\;` after a relation), so the pieces side by side are as wide as the formula drawn whole. The class of a symbol comes from SwiftUIMath's own tables (its patch 6). A formula with a style switch or an infix fraction (`\over`) at its outer level, or a piece that cannot be typeset, stays whole. The first piece copies the whole formula (`$…$`) and the others nothing; `AnyAttachment.continuesFormula` tells a host that a piece continues the formula before it (Graphite's read-aloud alignment counts the pieces as one equation). A table cell's narrowest width probe puts a line break before each later piece, so a column of long formulas shrinks to its widest piece. Upstream draws a formula as one attachment, which a line cannot break: a table of the owner's ("Capacitances by region", whose cells hold formulas such as `(C_{jb} \cdot L_A + C_{jsw})W + C_j \cdot W \cdot L/2`) was twice the note's width and scrolled, where Obsidian wraps it and it fits. Tests: `AppProjectTextualPatchTests.testInlineMathBreaksAfterOperatorsAndRelationsAtItsOuterLevelOnly`, `testFormulaInPiecesCopiesOnceAndKeepsItsWidth`, `testTableColumnOfLongFormulasShrinksToItsWidestPiece`, `testEveryWordGetsALineOfItsOwnExceptAcrossNonBreakingSpacesAndAttachments`, and `ReadAloudReadingViewTests.testFormulaDrawnInPiecesIsOneEquation`.

## 22. A line grows only by what its attachment needs

`Sources/Textual/Internal/Attachment/HangingAttachmentPlacement.swift` (new), `Internal/Attachment/AttachmentAttribute.swift`, `AttachmentView.swift`, `Internal/TextFragment/TextBuilder.swift`, `ReadingHighlight.swift`, `RoundedRunBackground.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/Shared/TextLinkInteraction.swift`, `TextLayout/LiveTextLayoutCollection.swift`: an attachment that hangs below the baseline, as a formula does, is set on a placeholder made of its part above the baseline, moved down only by the part of its descent the font's line does not already hold. Upstream sets the attachment's whole height with a baseline offset of its whole descent, and SwiftUI measures that line with an ascent of the image's whole height, as if the offset had not moved it up, and a descent of the font's descent plus the offset, even when the font's descent had room (measured on macOS 27 at 17 points: an image of height 21.6 with offset -7 gives ascent 22 and descent 11, where the image needs 15 and 7; height 10 with offset -2 gives descent 6, where the font's 4 was enough). So every formula with any descent pushed its line apart, by up to its descent twice over. The placeholder is no longer where the attachment is, so `Text.Layout.Run.contentBounds` says where it is, for the attachment's view, the reading highlight, rounded backgrounds, links and selection's hit testing. That frame has the attachment's exact size and baseline, where the placeholder's bounds were rounded up to a whole pixel. Display math (`MathAttachment.DisplayStyle.block`) keeps the room it had, since it is a block of its own and that room is part of how far it stands from the text around it. A smaller font on the placeholder would have made the font's descent irrelevant without asking for it (`fontLineDescent`, from `Font.resolve(in:)`), and a line holding only a small formula would then have lost the height of a line of text. An image of height 0 is drawn by SwiftUI at 32 points, so a placeholder is at least 1 point tall. On systems without `Font.resolve(in:)` the font's descent counts as 0; Graphite does not run on them. Tests: `HangingAttachmentPlacementTests` and `AppProjectTextualPatchTests.testInlineFractionsAndLimitsKeepTheirLineLowInTheReadingView`.

## 23. A run's rounded background is as tall as its text

`Sources/Textual/RoundedRunBackground.swift`, `Internal/TextFragment/TextBuilder.swift`, `Internal/Attachment/HangingAttachmentPlacement.swift`: behind an attachment, a `RoundedRunBackground` covers the attachment's width and its font's height around the baseline (`FontVerticalExtent`), not the attachment's own height. A web page draws the background of an inline element the same way: in Chromium, a `<mark>` holding an inline block 37 points tall at 17-point text has a box 20 points tall. Upstream has no such background; patch 19's took the union of its runs' bounds, so one `\dfrac` in a themed highlight made the highlight 37 points tall along its whole line (measured). The font's ascent and descent, unrounded, are what `Text.Layout.Run.typographicBounds` reports for a run of text in that font, so a line with words and formulas has one straight edge. The font lookup runs only for an attachment inside such a background. Graphite's parser now draws its own highlight this way too, since SwiftUI's `backgroundColor` draws for a run's text and a placeholder image is not text; a shape over the placeholder alone would meet SwiftUI's rectangles, which end on whole points, with seams in a translucent color. Tests: `HighlightBehindFormulaTests`, reading the pixels.

## 26. Inline math pieces for other text views

`Sources/Textual/InlineMathPieces.swift` (new), `Internal/Attachment/InlineMathLineBreaks.swift`: public `InlineMathPieces.pieces(of:)` cuts a formula where patch 21 cuts it, and gives each piece as the range of its characters in the formula with the space TeX puts after the operator that ends it (`spaceAfterOperator`, `\>` or `\;`, empty for the last piece); nil where patch 21 keeps the formula whole. `InlineMathLineBreaks.cuts(of:)` gives the places to cut, which `pieces(of:)` now builds its strings from. Graphite's Live Preview editor draws a long `$…$` of its own text in these pieces, each over its part of the hidden source, so a paragraph's formula wraps after its operators as the reading view's and tables' do; upstream has no inline math outside `StructuredText`, and patch 3 drew such a formula as one image whose room a line could not break. Test: `AppProjectTextualPatchTests.testInlineMathPiecesGiveTheReadingViewsPiecesAsRangesOfTheFormula` (the pieces are the reading view's, cover the formula once, Unicode outside the Basic Multilingual Plane included).

## 27. Selection gestures made on first touch

`Internal/TextInteraction/UIKit/UITextInteractionView.swift`: the selection's `UITextInteraction`, the tap that follows links and the link gestures of patches 12 and 24 are made and added the first time a touch, the pointer or Apple Pencil's hover lands on the view (`hitTest(_:with:)`, which UIKit calls before it gathers the recognizers that may take that touch), not when the view is made. Upstream made a dozen gesture recognizers for every text as it came on screen, about a third of the main thread's work of making a text in Graphite's reading view (`ReadingTextBlockCostHostedTests`: 2.1 to 1.8 ms a heading or paragraph in the iPad simulator), although few texts a scroll brings in are ever touched. Selection begins only by those gestures, so a text that is never touched never needs them. Tests: `ReadingLinkFollowingTests`, `PagePreviewCardHostedTests` and `ReadingTasksAndEquationsTests` tap, hold and select text through synthesized touches.

## 28. A fragment's text is built in the update that shows it, and its overlays read geometry only where needed

`Internal/TextFragment/TextFragment.swift`, `RoundedRunBackground.swift`, `Internal/Attachment/AttachmentOverlay.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/Shared/TextLinkInteraction.swift`: `TextFragment` builds its `TextBuilder` in the view update that first shows it, kept in a holder its state does not observe (`TextBuilderHolder`, made again only when the content changes), where upstream built it in `onChange`, so that every fragment was laid out once empty and again with its text. The rounded backgrounds of patch 13, the attachment overlay and the link tap make their geometry readers only for a fragment that has a run with a rounded background, an attachment or a link.

## 29. One block is shown without the block stack

`Internal/StructuredText/BlockContent.swift`: content of one block (a heading, a paragraph) is shown as that block, without `BlockVStack`, whose layout and spacing preferences place a block beside another; the reading view's texts are one block each.

## 30. Structured text is parsed in the update that shows it

`StructuredText/StructuredText.swift`: `StructuredText` parses its markup in the view update that first shows it, kept in a holder its state does not observe (`ParsedMarkup`, parsed again only when the markup changes). Upstream parsed it in `onChange(of:initial:)`, which runs after that update, so every structured text was first laid out empty (a table or a formula at 0 points) and then again with its blocks. As upstream, a new parser alone does not parse again.

## 31. A fragment's text is styled in the update that shows it

`Internal/InlineText/WithInlineStyle.swift`: the inline style (code, emphasis, strong, strikethrough, links) is applied in the update that first shows the text, kept in a holder its state does not observe (`StyledText`, made again only when the input, the style or the text environment changes). Upstream applied it in `onChange`, so every `TextFragment` was first laid out with no text at all, and the block around it a second time.

## 32. Text and measurements that did not change change no view state

`Internal/TextFragment/TextBuilder.swift`: `proposalChanged` keeps the text when the attachment sizes are the ones it was built with; the container's size reported again set the observed `text` to the same text and drew it again. `StructuredText/Style/Overflow.swift`: the widths that decide whether the content needs the scroll view (`OverflowWidths`) are kept where no view observes them; as state, the first measurements of a table that fits laid it out a second time. `Internal/StructuredText/Table.swift`: the cell spacing preference is set as state only when it differs.

Measured on the iPad simulator (iOS 27.2, Release, `PerformanceBenchmarkTests.testOpeningScrollingAndTypingInALongNote`): with patches 30 to 32 and Graphite's own reading at hand (`LivePreviewNoteReadingModifier.readingAtHand`), a table, a callout or a display formula scrolling in is laid out once in its first frame, where it was laid out four times. Found on the way, and left as it was: `ObsidianTableStyle`'s `tableCellSpacing(horizontal: 1, vertical: 1)` never reaches the table (the preference arrives empty), so tables are spaced by `TableColumnsLayout.defaultCellSpacing` (8 points); making it arrive would change how every table looks.

## 33. A list is laid out at its final height the first time

`Internal/StructuredText/BlockVStack.swift`, `Internal/StructuredText/OrderedList.swift`: a list's items are spaced by the list item spacing read from the environment, where the list puts it (`resolvedListItemSpacing`), instead of from the block spacing preference; upstream read it in `onPreferenceChange`, so the first pass spaced the items by their views' own spacing and a second by the list's (a three-item list 60 points tall, then 68.5). A numbered list's markers are each laid out as wide as the list's largest ordinal's, kept hidden behind the marker, which for the decimal marker (monospaced digits) is the widest: upstream laid each marker out at its own width and lined them up in a second pass, which laid every item's text out again at its new width (twelve wrapped items 528 points tall, then 574.75). The second pass still comes when the markers come out of different widths, as other ordinal markers can. Text of several blocks that is not a list, such as a paragraph followed by a list, took a second pass for the spacing between its blocks until patch 36. Pictures of nine lists (bulleted, numbered to 12, numbered from 8, nested, numbered nested, loose, tasks, after a paragraph) drawn with the old and the new code are the same pixels. Test: `TextualFirstLayoutTests.testAListIsLaidOutAtItsFinalHeightTheFirstTime`, failing for all five of its lists without the patch.

## 34. The reading highlight's frames reported to a receiver, not through a preference

`ReadingHighlight.swift`: a text drawing the word read aloud reports its frames to the `ReadingHighlightReceiver` the host puts in the environment (`readingHighlightReceiver`), by the word's range, and reports none for that range once its highlight goes; the receiver tells the host every frame drawn now. Upstream's `ReadingHighlightGeometryKey` preference is gone: observed around a lazy stack, it was reduced over every block at every update, whether or not a word was read. Measured on an iPad simulator (Docs/Reading-view-speed-todo.md, section 1): a note of code blocks scrolled with 13 to 32 frames late from the main thread's work before, 0 to 3 after; a reading block 6.1 times a plain `Text` before, 4.4 times after.

Remove this vendored copy and return to the upstream package once an upstream release contains equivalents of these changes.

## 35. Attachments zoomed with the host's text

`Sources/Textual/TextEnvironmentValues.swift`, `Sources/Textual/View+Textual.swift`: `TextEnvironmentValues.attachmentScale`, set with `.textual.attachmentScale(_:)` (1 by default), reaches an attachment's `sizeThatFits(_:in:)`, so a host that zooms its text can zoom the pictures inside it without building its text again. Being part of the hashed environment, a new scale lays the text out again. Graphite zooms its notes' pictures inside text with it (HUNT-388).

## 36. Text of several blocks is laid out at its final height the first time

`View+Textual.swift`, `Internal/StructuredText/BlockSpacingKey.swift`, `BlockVStack.swift`, `BlockQuote.swift`, `UnorderedList.swift`, `OrderedList.swift`: `textual.blockSpacing` also sets the spacing as a container value (`textualRequestedBlockSpacing`), which the block stack reads from its subviews in the update that makes them, so each block is spaced from the first pass. A block that requests none gives the union of the spacing its blocks request, as the preference does (`textualContainedBlockSpacing`): the block stack sets it on itself, and a block quote and a list item, whose styles hold their blocks inside views of their own, read their blocks as subviews (`Group(subviews:)`) and set it around the style's view. Upstream spaced the blocks by the `BlockSpacingKey` preference alone, read in `onPreferenceChange`, so text of several blocks that is not a list (a paragraph and a list, a quote of two paragraphs, a heading and its paragraph) was first spaced by its views' own spacing and moved in a second pass (a paragraph and a list in a callout 140.25 points tall, then 153.85). The preference is still read and wins when it differs, as for a style that requests its spacing inside a view of its own, out of the container values' reach. Pictures of 17 texts (quotes, lists, tables, headings, rules, code, formulas and tasks beside paragraphs, alone and in a callout) drawn with the old and the new code are the same pixels. Test: `TextualFirstLayoutTests.testTextOfSeveralBlocksIsLaidOutAtItsFinalHeightTheFirstTime`, failing for seven of its eight texts without the patch (the eighth, a callout of one paragraph, has no block stack).

## 37. Each text's highlight frames kept apart in the receiver

`ReadingHighlight.swift`: `ReadingHighlightReceiver` keeps the frames each text reported by that text (`report(_:of:from:)`, a `UUID` held in the modifier's state), no longer by the word's range alone. Patch 34 kept them by range, so in a table, where every cell's text reports for the word read, a cell after the word's own reported no frame and took the word's frames away. The highlight's frames of a Live Preview table then never reached the host (`ReadAloudReadingViewTests.testLivePreviewTableMathAndOpenCalloutHighlightActualRenderedContent`, failing since patch 34). A host that reports one text per word, as the reading view's numbered equations do, still reports by range.

Remove this vendored copy and return to the upstream package once an upstream release contains equivalents of these changes.

## 12. Links tell a host when the pointer rests on them

`Sources/Textual/TextLinkHovering.swift` (new), `Internal/TextInteraction/Shared/TextLayout/TextLayoutCollection+Geometry.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/Shared/TextSelectionModel.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/AppKit/AppKitTextInteractionOverlay.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/AppKit/NSTextInteractionView.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/UIKit/UIKitTextInteractionOverlay.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/UIKit/UITextInteractionView.swift`: public `textual.linkHoverAction(_:)` gives selectable text a `TextLinkHoverAction`, told `TextLinkHover.entered(URL, frame:)` when the pointer comes onto a link (the frame of the link's text under the pointer, in the window's own coordinates), `.exited(URL)` when it leaves, and `.pressed(URL, frame:)` when a link is held. Graphite shows its link preview cards with it (Page Preview). `TextLayoutCollection.link(for:)` finds the link under a point and the frame of its run, as `url(for:)` finds the link a click opens. On the Mac, `NSTextInteractionView` follows the pointer with a tracking area while an action is set, and only then; moving between the lines of one link is staying on it. On the iPad, `UITextInteractionView` adds a hover recognizer (a trackpad's or mouse's pointer, and Apple Pencil hovering) and a long press that begins only on a link, while an action is set: the selection's own gestures wait for that press, which receives only touches that start on a link, so holding a link shows its preview instead of selecting its word, and holding other text still selects it. Upstream has no way for a host to know which link the pointer is on.

## 24. Links with a host's own menu and modifier clicks

`Sources/Textual/TextLinkInteractions.swift` (new), `Internal/TextInteraction/AppKit/AppKitTextInteractionOverlay.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/AppKit/NSTextInteractionView.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/UIKit/UIKitTextInteractionOverlay.swift`, `Internal/TextInteraction/UIKit/UITextInteractionView.swift`: public `textual.linkInteractions(_:)` gives selectable text a `TextLinkInteractions`: the menu items a host gives a link (`TextLinkMenuItem`, a title, an SF Symbol and an action; none for a link the text's own menu serves), and what a tap or click on a link with modifier keys held does (true when the host handled it, so the link is not followed). Graphite gives a picture drawn in text, whose run links to its zoom, "Zoom In", "Open in New Tab" and "Open to the Right", and opens it in a new tab on a Command-click. On the Mac, a secondary click on such a link puts the host's items first in `NSTextInteractionView`'s menu without selecting the word under the pointer; a click passes `event.modifierFlags`. On the iPad, a long press on such a link (the same press that shows a link's preview) and a secondary click of a trackpad or mouse show the host's items as the system's edit menu (`UIEditMenuInteraction`, made the first time it is shown), and a tap passes its recognizer's `modifierFlags`. Upstream has no menu or modifier keys for links.

The secondary-click recognizer takes only a pointer's touches (`touch.type == .indirectPointer`): UIKit gives a finger's tap to a tap recognizer whatever its `buttonMaskRequired`, so on the iPad a tap on a picture inside text, whose link has the host's menu, showed that menu instead of zooming (HUNT-382, `PictureZoomAndTabHostedTests.testAFingersTapOnAPictureInsideASentenceZoomsIt`).

## 25. Wide display math scaled to its column on paper

`Sources/Textual/MathProperties.swift`, `Internal/Attachment/MathAttachment.swift`: `MathProperties.wideDisplayMath` says what block math wider than its column does: `.brokenIntoLines` (the default, as before) or `.scaledToFit`, which keeps the formula on one line and scales it down uniformly to the column's width, as a printed page shows a wide picture. The attachment measures as its natural size scaled to the proposed width, and its view draws the formula at its natural size under a scale transform (`ScaledDownToItsFrame`), so its outlines stay vectors. Graphite's PDF export sets it (`ReadingTextPrinting` in `MarkdownPreview.swift`). Broken into lines on paper, a long derivation came apart at odd places (a `\text{using …}` split inside its word, a line overhanging the column's right edge), and a centered formula measured again at the width it had been broken to narrowed, drawing after drawing, into a column of fragments a few symbols wide. Upstream has no such choice. Test: `NotePDFFormulasAndEmbedsTests.testAWideDisplayFormulaIsScaledOntoOneLineInsideTheColumn`, reading the printed page's pixels.
